Author: anfroholic
Content:
Hey all, I will be meeting with the place that's dicing the wafers. Again this time, they're requesting we back-grind the wafers. We're looking to reduce costs as best we can. 
I have a list of questions here. Can anyone think of any better (more) questions to ask? 

-----

- What saw street widths would allow us to dice without backgrinding?
- What width for multi pass cut?
- What width for single pass cut?
- If we are able to provide 250um would that be sufficient?

- What types of saws exist and what type of trade offs between them?


- What information is most useful when planning dicing schemes
  - Is single reticle detail, and general reticle in wafer sufficient? 
  - Would another filetype be better?   DXF, etc? 

- What is the primary driver of cost? Dicing time? Config set up? Saw type?

- How is pricing structured: per wafer, per cut, per program setup, per die picked? 
- What's a one-time cost versus a recurring cost? 

Thanks!!

Author: anfroholic
Content:
Agreed, I think my frame of questioning basically sounds like...
Thicker wheels can more aggressively cut -- BUT these larger wheels chip more. (some of my experience as a machinist)
This also means consumables costs go down, machine cost goes down
But the cost in silicon goes up (larger saw street) 

I'm sure we'll go around and around and they won't give me an answer, I've done this before, but in the end I think they'll guide us towards our optimal solution.

Content:
When I was meeting with Poh I asked first, "do you know anyone at Kulicke & Soffa" as they are headquartered near my hotel and they make the (best, most, one of those words) wirebonders and he said no. 
I then asked  "do you know *any* wirebonders?"

I obviously said yes lol. 
The guy didn't really have a lot of useful information that was sharable. He sent me to this [product](https://www.yamaha-robotics.com/en/products/process/utc-rz1) and while it does have specs it wasn't what I was hoping for. 

The one dimension I kept asking about was the length based on die height. The spec we used said 1.5x height, @stuart said 2x, but this guy was very adamant those were wrong and you can go super close, it depends on the capillary you get. He drew some stuff on the whiteboard for me and then erased it before I could take a pic. He then pointed me at this company [SPT](https://www.smallprecisiontools.com/shortcuts-en/publications-downloads/semiconductor-bonding-tools-downloads/?oid=120&lang=en) There's a bunch of stuff to read there, but haven't clicked a link, but they sell the capillaries.
